FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the differences between the types of kyphosis.
Recognize common physical examination findings in patients with kyphosis.
Describe the role of appropriate baseline and advanced imaging studies.
Review the indications for nonsurgical and surgical management of kyphosis.
Overview
Thoracic kyphosis is an apex posterior convex curvature in the sagittal plane of the thoracic
spine, with a normal value ranging from 10° to 40°.
The thoracolumbar junction (T10 through L2) usually is free of kyphosis or lordosis.
Kyphosis of more than 40° in the thoracic spine or of more than 10° in the thoracolumbar
spine may be considered abnormal.


Overview
Normal sagittal alignment of the mobile portion of the human spine includes cervical
and lumbar lordosis and thoracic kyphosis. Multiple causes exist for the variations in
normal sagittal alignment. The term kyphosis comes from ancient Greece, where Galen
of Pergamon (130 to 200 AD) used the term to describe a backward kyphus or hump
shape of the spine.1
Evaluation
Patient History
Age of onset and rate of progression are critical in determining patient prognosis.
Congenital scoliosis may be associated with abnormalities, such as cardiac, neurologic, or
renal malformations; these malformations should be evaluated simultaneously.
Concurrent syndromes, diseases, or genetic disorders may cause kyphosis, and they also
should be evaluated carefully.

Patient History
In evaluating kyphosis, a careful patient history is paramount. Patient age or the timing
of onset may be critical in making other potential underlying diagnoses, such as renal or
cardiac abnormalities, in very young children with kyphosis. Associated symptoms, such
as headaches or radicular pain, are important indicators of potential underlying
intraspinal abnormalities, such as a Chiari malformation or syringomyelia. The rapidity of
progression may indicate the type of kyphosis. Other known medical conditions, such as
abdominal or spinal cord tumors; neuromuscular or genetic disorders; and potential
infectious etiologies, such as tuberculosis, need to be well documented.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
2/21

Evaluation of the skin also can help determine the cause of kyphosis.
A thorough neurologic examination is necessary to determine red flags for possible concurrent
intraspinal abnormalities.

Physical Examination
A thorough physical examination must include inspection of the skin to assess for signs
of spinal dysraphism, striae, or café au lait spots, in addition to assessing the deformity.
Clinical flexibility of the kyphosis should be documented, and the spine should be
assessed for scoliosis. Performing a careful neurologic examination that includes muscle
strength and sensation is necessary. Deep tendon reflexes and the abdominal reflex
should be well documented. In young children, cardiac auscultation also should be
performed to evaluate for possible associated cardiac abnormalities. Lower extremity
flexibility should be assessed. Patients with hyperlordosis and/or tight hamstrings should
be evaluated carefully for concomitant spondylolisthesis. Foot deformities may lead to
other diagnoses, such as hereditary motor sensory neuropathy (cavus foot) or
connective tissue disease (pes planovalgus).
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Radiography
Plain radiographs should include standing or sitting AP and lateral views of the cervical,
thoracic, and lumbar spine. The radiographs should include the hip so proper sagittal
analysis parameters, including pelvic incidence, can be measured. Radiographs usually
are sufficient to document the type and degree of kyphosis. Upright lateral radiographs
should be interpreted with caution in children because 3 mm of anterior wedging may
be a normal finding. Obtaining a supine lateral hyperextension radiograph over a bolster
placed at the apex of the kyphosis may help determine the flexibility of the curve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
3/21

Flexion/extension lateral radiographs may be useful in determining instability of a
kyphotic segment.2
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI typically is necessary only in patients in whom neurologic abnormalities are noted on
physical examination or in patients with congenital kyphosis in whom the incidence of
intraspinal anomalies, such as syringomyelia, tethered cord, or Chiari malformations, are
common.
MRI also may aid in understanding the extent of disease in patients with underlying infection
or neoplastic processes.
Computed Tomography
CT may aid in better understanding the abnormal bony anatomy in patients with congenital
kyphosis.
CT scans also are valuable for preoperative planning but are associated with radiation
exposure.
Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is infrequently performed but may be helpful in evaluating
children with poor bone density who may require surgical treatment.
Bone Age Evaluation
A hand radiograph for bone age aids in predicting remaining growth and the potential for
disease progression.
Special Tests
Echocardiography and renal ultrasonography are routinely performed in young children in
whom congenital scoliosis is suspected to rule out associated abnormalities.
Pulmonary function tests are useful in children with neuromuscular scoliosis.
Laboratory tests are useful if infection or a neoplasm is suspected.


Special Tests
Nonimaging studies typically are not necessary in the evaluation of patients with
kyphosis; however, children with congenital kyphosis should undergo a thorough cardiac
and renal evaluation, which may require echocardiography and/or renal
ultrasonography to rule out associated abnormalities. Children with features concerning
for connective tissue disease should undergo genetic evaluation to help guide treatment.
Pulmonary function tests should be considered in children with neuromuscular
kyphoscoliosis. If concern exists for an infectious or neoplastic process, a complete
blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, or
tuberculin skin test may be warranted (Resource 1).
Classification
Intrinsic Types
Postural kyphosis
Diagnosis of exclusion
Imaging often is unnecessary if kyphosis is clinically flexible and no other warning signs are
present.
Scheuermann kyphosis
Defined as three consecutive vertebrae or more with 5° or greater kyphosis
Incidence of 1% to 8% of general population; more common in males.
Unknown etiology but may involve disordered growth of the anterior vertebral endplates
Physical examination findings include a rounded apical kyphosis, usually in the thoracic
spine, best observed on forward bending; some degree of scoliosis also may be present.
Nonsurgical treatment, including thoracolumbosacral orthosis bracing, is reserved for
smaller curves and skeletally immature children.
Surgical treatment is reserved for patients with curves greater than 80°, intractable pain, or
progression despite brace wear.
Neuromuscular and syndromic disorders
Common neuromuscular conditions that may cause kyphosis include myelodysplasia, caudal
regression syndrome, and spinal muscular atrophy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
5/21

Common syndromes include connective tissue diseases, such as Marfan syndrome;
mucopolysaccharidoses; and some skeletal dysplasias, such as spondylometaphyseal
dysplasia.6
Curve flexibility, the rate of progression, and global alignment of the patient often determine
the likelihood of surgical treatment.
Nonsurgical management includes wheelchair adjustment and management of skin
concerns for non-ambulating neuromuscular patients.
Bracing may delay surgical management but usually is not curative.
Surgical treatment should be considered in patients with a rigid, progressive deformity and
patients in whom skin integrity is at risk.
Preoperative halo-gravity traction may be required in patients with a large curve.
Skin coverage should be carefully evaluated in patients who undergo surgical treatment to
prevent postoperative wound coverage issues.
Congenital kyphosis
Most likely caused by a genetic defect in the process of somitogenesis between weeks five
and eight in utero
Type 1 congenital kyphosis (failure of formation) is the most dangerous type because it may
cause a sharp, rigid kyphosis over a single segment, leading to possible neurologic
compromise.
A thorough neurologic examination is necessary to assess for upper motor neuron long tract
signs of possible neurologic compromise.
MRI and CT are routinely performed to evaluate morphology and to aid in preoperative
planning.
Bracing is not indicated in this patient population.
Well-balanced curves without neurologic compromise can be managed via posterior spine
instrumentation and fusion without decompression.
Large kyphotic curves associated with neurologic symptoms are best managed via
decompression of the neural elements, restoration of sagittal balance via spinal osteotomy,
and posterior spine fusion with instrumentation.

Intrinsic Types
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
6/21

Postural kyphosis is benign but is a diagnosis of exclusion made by ruling out more
potentially problematic disorders. Clinically, these patients present with excessive
thoracic kyphosis of a gentle, rounded nature (also known as round kyphosis) without
apical deformity.3,4 Pain, if present, typically is muscular in nature without radicular
symptoms. Imaging studies typically are not necessary unless the kyphosis is rigid
clinically or if other warning signs are noted in the patient history or physical
examination. Surgeons should be aware of potential undiagnosed connective tissue
disorders (ie, Marfan syndrome), which may have a similar presentation. These patients
may exhibit other chest wall anomalies, such as pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum.
Scheuermann disease is defined radiographically by the Sorenson criteria:
hyperkyphosis, three or more consecutive vertebra with anterior wedging of 5°, and
endplate irregularities. The incidence ranges from 1% to 8% of the population, with a
slight predilection in males (2 to 7:1 ratio). The disorder most commonly affects the
thoracic spine (typical); however, the disorder also can occur in the thoracolumbar and
lumbar (atypical) spine.5 The etiology remains unknown but may involve a disorder of
the vertebral endplate resulting in an overall lack of anterior vertebral body growth.
Evaluation and diagnosis are based on the patient history, physical examination findings,
and imaging studies. Advanced imaging studies are not warranted unless neurologic
abnormalities are noted on physical examination. The hallmark physical examination
finding is an A-frame appearance at the apex of the kyphosis on the forward bend test
(Figure 1). Striae of the dorsal skin also may be present (Figure 2). Standing AP and
lateral radiographs typically demonstrate a mild scoliosis with hyperkyphosis of the
involved segment, as described in the Sorenson criteria (Figure 3, A). A hyperextension
lateral radiograph of the spine over a bolster may aid in assessing preoperative flexibility
(Figure 3, B).

Figure 3 Lateral radiographs of the spine of a 13-year-old girl with Scheuermann
disease. A, Standing radiograph demonstrates apical wedging of the vertebra, endplate
irregularities, and hyperkyphosis (Cobb angle greater than 90°). The C7 plumb line falls
well posterior to S1. B, Supine radiograph over a bolster demonstrates that the curve is
quite rigid, with very little change in the Cobb angle compared with the standing
radiograph. (Courtesy of Robert Kamiel Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)
Management depends on skeletal maturity and curve magnitude. Observation typically
is recommended for thoracic curves less than 60°. Bracing is recommended for skeletally
immature patients (lower than Risser grade 4) who have curves greater than 60°; bracing
should be continued through skeletal maturity.
Surgical indications for thoracic curves include progression despite brace wear in
skeletally immature patients, curves greater than 80°, or intractable pain.3,5 Surgical
indications are less clear in patients with an atypical (thoracolumbar) curve because
curve magnitude may be much less. These curves tend to be more painful despite
nonsurgical management. Fusion levels for thoracic curves must include the proximal
Cobb angle, and some studies suggest starting at T2 to minimize the risk of proximal
junctional kyphosis.5The distal fusion level typically is the vertebra just caudal to the first
lordotic disk but should include the sagittal stable vertebra5 (Figure 4). Historically,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
9/21

surgical management included a combined anterior and posterior approach; however,
more modern instrumentation has allowed surgeons to achieve optimal results via
posterior-only approaches. Most surgeons recommend correcting no more than 50% of
the deformity to decrease the risk of junctional issues proximal and distal to spinal
instrumentation (Resource 2).
Figure 4 Standing lateral radiographs of the spine of a patient with Scheuermann
disease. A, The sagittal stable vertebra is L2. B, Radiograph obtained 2 years after
posterior spine fusion. (Courtesy of Robert Kamiel Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)
Neuromuscular and syndromic disorders encompass a wide variety of pathologies that
may result in kyphosis or kyphoscoliosis. Common neuromuscular conditions associated
with kyphosis include myelodysplasia, caudal regression syndrome, and spinal muscular
atrophy. Common syndromes include connective tissue diseases, such as Marfan
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
10/21

syndrome; mucopolysaccharidoses; and some skeletal dysplasias, such as
spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. The severity of kyphosis also varies with the underlying
etiology. Children with mucopolysaccharidosis have a gibbus deformity that remains
relatively flexible, whereas patients with high-level myelodysplasia may have a very rigid
gibbus deformity (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Standing lateral radiograph of the spine of an 8-year-old girl demonstrates
thoracic-level myelodysplasia and a severe, rigid gibbus deformity. (Courtesy of Robert
Kamiel Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)
The etiology of the kyphosis is associated with the underlying diagnosis and imbalance of
trunk muscle tone. Evaluation includes a thorough patient history and physical
examination. The flexibility of the curve and the integrity of the skin over the apex of the
kyphosis should be well documented. Upright standing or sitting radiographs should be
obtained if possible.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
11/21

Treatment hinges on optimizing a patient’s health in terms of the underlying disorder via
a multidisciplinary team approach. Proper seating for full-time wheelchair users is
necessary. Monitoring skin integrity over the apex of the deformity is necessary in
children without sensation at that level. Bracing may delay surgical management but is
not curative.
Surgical management should be considered in patients with a rigid, progressive
deformity or in patients in whom skin integrity is at risk7 (Figure 6). Severe curves may
benefit from preoperative traction for a period of weeks. A rigid gibbus deformity
requires complete kyphectomy, whereas flexible deformities can be corrected via a
posterior-only approach (Figure 7). Preoperative consultation with a plastic surgeon is
helpful because wound closure may be complex, especially in children with
myelodysplasia who have undergone previous flap coverage.
Figure 6 Lateral (A) and posterior (B) view intraoperative photographs of the spine of an
8-year-old girl show thoracic-level myelodysplasia and a severe, rigid gibbus deformity.
(Courtesy of Robert Kamiel Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)

Figure 7 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) standing lateral radiographs of the spine
of an 8-year-old girl with thoracic-level myelodysplasia and a severe, rigid gibbus
deformity managed via kyphectomy and posterior fusion. (Courtesy of Robert Kamiel
Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)
Congenital kyphosis most likely results from a genetic defect in the process of
somitogenesis between weeks five and eight in utero. It is classified as failure of
formation (type 1), a failure of segmentation (type 2), a failure of formation and
segmentation (type 3), or unclassifiable (as in a congenital spine dislocation [type 4,
Figure 8]). Type 1 anomalies are the most dangerous because they cause a sharp, rigid
kyphosis over one or two segments. Dissimilar from other forms of kyphosis, spastic
paraparesis can occur in as many as 10% of untreated patients.8,9 This most commonly
involves type 1 anomalies in the upper thoracic (watershed) area of the spine. A
thorough patient history and physical examination, focusing on neurologic examination,
is necessary. Imaging studies should include upright AP and lateral radiographs of the
cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine. MRI is warranted because of the relatively high
likelihood of spinal cord compression. CT is not necessary for diagnosis but may aid in

13/21

preoperative planning. Bracing is not effective in patients with this condition. Early
surgical management is warranted for progressive cases. Posterior spine
instrumentation and fusion across the involved segment is adequate for prophylactic
treatment in young children without neurologic compromise or upper motor neuron
signs. Decompression with fusion is necessary in patients with clinical or radiographic
evidence of spinal cord compression. Often, this treatment requires exposure and
decompression of the neural elements, three-column spinal osteotomy, and posterior
spine fusion with instrumentation to realign the spine. Careful neuromonitoring is
paramount because spinal cord ischemia can occur during these procedures.
Figure 8 Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the spine of a 20-month-old boy with caudal
regression syndrome demonstrates a congenital spine dislocation. (Courtesy of Robert
Kamiel Lark, MD, FAAOS, Raleigh, NC.)
Extrinsic Types
Trauma
Flexion/distraction injury (Chance fracture) from a motor vehicle collision is the most
common type of injury that results in kyphosis and can occur at any location in the spine.
Clinical equipoise exists about whether remodeling of these injuries can occur.SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
14/21

Infection or neoplasm
Both are marked by destruction of the vertebral body and/or the intervertebral disk, leading
to collapse and kyphosis.
Tuberculosis is the most common cause of spinal infection in children worldwide.
Spinal tumors are rare in children but may cause kyphosis as the vertebral body is destroyed
Tumors rarely affect the intervertebral disk because it is avascular.
Iatrogenic factors
Post-radiation kyphosis is a complication typically resulting from the radiation management
of intrabdominal or spinal tumors.
Post-laminectomy kyphosis results from disruption of the posterior column without
adequate repair and immobilization.
Instrumentation-related kyphosis (ie, proximal or distal junctional kyphosis) has a
multifactorial etiology.

Extrinsic Types
Posttraumatic kyphosis typically result from a flexion/distraction type injury (Chance
fracture) and can occur in the cervical, thoracic, or lumbar regions. Few studies have
been published on this topic because these injuries are relatively rare.10 Schwarz et al11
reported that six of eight children who underwent nonsurgical treatment of a cervical
spine injury had persistent kyphosis of more than 10°. The authors proposed that the
flexion injury resulted in compaction of the cancellous bone that could not remodel. The
authors suggested that surgical management via anterior strut grafting and plating or
posterior wiring was necessary to prevent permanent deformity. Conversely, Ogden12,13
reported remodeling potential in thoracic and lumbar compression fractures
proportional to the severity of the injury and the age of the child if the vertebral endplate
was not damaged.
Infection and neoplasm may result in destruction of the vertebral body and/or the
intervertebral disk, resulting in kyphosis. Aggressive medical management of the
underlying process is necessary, and orthopaedic management initially involving proper
immobilization.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Kyphosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000526
15/21

Tuberculosis remains the most common cause of spinal infection in young children
worldwide. In the United States, spinal tuberculosis is much rarer. Therefore, other
infections, such as those from Staphylococcus aureus and the Streptococcus species, are
much more common. Early in the disease process, the kyphosis remains flexible and
responsive to bracing. Later in the disease process, the kyphosis becomes more rigid
and less amenable to nonsurgical management. Surgical management is warranted for
fixed angular deformity or for neurologic changes resulting from anterior epidural
abscess. Anterior decompression and strut grafting are necessary in such cases because
laminectomy alone does not decompress the abscess and leads to additional posterior
instability and worsening deformity. This treatment is followed by posterior
instrumentation and prolonged pharmacologic management.14
Spinal tumors are exceedingly rare in children but may result in destruction of the
anterior spinal column and kyphosis. Tumors require a substantial blood supply to
thrive; therefore, they rarely affect the intervertebral disk, which is avascular. If the
tumor involves the pedicle or facet joints, lateral or rotational deformities may occur.
Flexion/extension radiographs may aid in determining the stability of the involved
segment. Surgical management typically necessitates anterior column support (ie, strut
grafting or an interbody cage) with posterior fixation.15
The iatrogenic causes of kyphosis can be broadly divided into three categories: post-
radiation kyphosis, post-laminectomy kyphosis, and instrumentation-related kyphosis.
Post-radiation kyphosis is a complication that typically results from radiation
management of intrabdominal or spinal tumors. The radiation dose may interfere with
anterior growth of the vertebral body and/or result in fibrosis of the anterior
ligamentous complex and musculature, exacerbating kyphotic deformity. In a report by
de Jonge et al,15 46 of 63 children treated via radiation therapy with or without
laminectomy or laminoplasty required surgical treatment for iatrogenic kyphosis. All but
nine of the children initially were treated nonsurgically via rigid bracing. Preoperative
traction was used for rigid deformities. Surgical correction was obtained via posterior
spinal fusion in seven patients; the other patients required anterior and posterior fusion.
The authors recommended extending the fusion well beyond the irradiation field to
minimize the risk of junctional issues.

Post-laminectomy kyphosis results from disruption of the posterior column without
adequate repair and immobilization. Children who undergo such procedures must be
monitored closely for kyphosis. If possible, laminoplasty should be performed in lieu of
laminectomy, with prolonged rigid immobilization, to delay the development of
deformity until adequate spinal growth has been achieved. Posterolateral fusion with
instrumentation often is required. A rigid brace should be used for a minimum of 6
months postoperatively in patients with poor bone quality.
Instrumentation-related kyphosis refers to the development of kyphosis at the proximal
(proximal junctional kyphosis) or distal (distal junctional kyphosis) junction at which
spinal instrumentation ends.
Proximal junctional kyphosis has been defined as kyphosis of more than 10° measured
from the lower endplate of the upper instrumented vertebra to the superior endplate
two levels above on postoperative radiographs compared with the same levels on
preoperative radiographs. It can occur with anterior or posterior instrumentation (Figure
9). The exact cause of this complication remains unknown but is associated with many
risk factors, including an improper selection of fusion levels, pseudarthrosis, inadequate
restoration of sagittal balance, an underlying diagnosis, excessive preoperative
hyperkyphosis, the location of proximal anchors (ie, rib based versus spine based), and
iatrogenic disruption of posterior anatomy (eg, adjacent facet capsule, interspinous
ligaments).16,17

Figure 9 Standing lateral radiographs of the spine of a 16-year-old boy with spastic

Distal junctional kyphosis is defined as kyphosis of more than 10° measured from the
superior endplate of the lower instrumented vertebra to the inferior endplate of the
level below on postoperative radiographs compared with the same levels on
preoperative radiographs. This complication is observed more rarely than proximal
junctional kyphosis. Risk factors for distal junctional kyphosis depend on the underlying
etiology necessitating spinal fusion. It can occur with anterior or posterior
instrumentation. Inclusion of the sagittal stable vertebra in the construct minimizes the
risk of distal junctional kyphosis.18
